newsitem.title: HONDURAS: GDP in CentAm countries grows by average of 3 pct.
newsitem.headline: GDP in CentAm countries grows by average of 3 pct.

text.p: The gross domestic products of six poor Central American countries grew by an average of 3.0 percent in 1996, according to a report by the Economic Commission for Latin American and the Caribbean (CEPAL).

The poorest of the poor, Nicaragua, posted the highest growth rate, 5.5 percent, while the best off of Central American countries, Costa Rica, had the lowest GDP growth at 0.5 percent, according to the report, which was published Tuesday in the Honduran newspaper El Herado.
The economies of Honduras and El Salvador grew by 3.5 percent each while Guatemala's GDP grew by 3.0 percent in 1996, the report said.
In Panama, a country geographically in Central America but not closely tied to the other five, the GDP grew by 2.0 percent.

Costa Rica, the so-called Switzerland of Central America, merely continued its economic slump of recent years, CEPAL said, calling it "the most critical period since the early 1980s," before the Costa Rican economy began to take off.
The five main Central American countries depend heavily on coffee exports and to lesser and varying degrees on other agricultural products, tourism and duty-free textile exports.
CEPEL attributed Nicaragua's growth to democratic advances and the former government's discipline in maintaining a tight monetary and fiscal policy despite that 1996 was an election year.

But a tight monetary policy worked to the detriment of GDP growth in El Salvador, CEPAL said, adding that the country also was hit hard by lower world coffee prices and lower demand from Central American neighbors for Salvadoran export products.
El Salvador posted GDP growth of 6.1 percent in 1995.
The Honduran GDP grew by 3.5 percent for the second straight year, bolstered by modest increases in exports and internal investment and consumption, CEPAL said.

In Guatemala, growth fell to three percent from five percent in 1995 because of tighter monetary and fiscal policy and lower world coffee prices. Also, lagging economies in Costa Rica and El Salvador lowered demand for Guatemalan exports, CEPAL said.
